  <p class="eyebrow">Research</p>
  <h1>Mathematical structure, computation and applications</h1>
  <p>My research connects rigorous analysis with algorithms and applied models. It has developed through three main themes: optimisation and inverse problems, PDEs and materials, and statistical modelling for decision-making.</p>
</header>

<section class="research-introduction-refined">
  <div>
    <p class="eyebrow">Research approach</p>
    <h2>From theory to methods that can be tested</h2>
  </div>
  <p>I am interested in problems where structure matters: data may be incomplete, systems may evolve over time, or the quantity of interest may not be directly observable. I use mathematical analysis to understand the problem, optimisation and statistics to construct methods, and computation to test their behaviour. The result may be a theorem, an algorithm, a model or a decision rule—but the underlying aim is the same: reliable conclusions from difficult information.</p>
</section>

<section class="research-theme-refined" id="inverse-problems-research">
  <div class="research-theme-number">01</div>
  <div class="research-theme-heading">
    <p class="eyebrow">Optimisation · Inverse problems · Imaging</p>
    <h2>Recovering dynamic structure from incomplete data</h2>
  </div>
  <div class="research-theme-body">
    <p>During my postdoctoral research at the University of Graz, I helped develop a framework for reconstructing time-dependent sources from noisy, severely undersampled measurements. The work combines optimal-transport regularisation with generalized conditional-gradient methods, allowing moving sources to be represented sparsely and updated through interpretable trajectories.</p>
    <p>The programme developed from functional analysis and well-posedness theory to convergence analysis, algorithm design and numerical experiments for dynamic MRI and Fourier measurements.</p>
    <dl class="research-contributions">
      <div><dt>Question</dt><dd>How can motion be reconstructed when each time point contains only a small and noisy fraction of the required data?</dd></div>
      <div><dt>Contribution</dt><dd>Dynamic regularisation models, sparse optimisation algorithms and convergence guarantees.</dd></div>
      <div><dt>Methods</dt><dd>Optimal transport, convex analysis, conditional gradients, measure-valued optimisation and numerical simulation.</dd></div>
    </dl>
    <p class="research-links-refined"><a href="publications.html#2023-Bre-Car-Fan-Rom">Foundations of Computational Mathematics →</a><a href="https://github.com/sfanzon/DGCG_algorithm">Code →</a></p>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="research-theme-refined" id="materials-research">
  <div class="research-theme-number">02</div>
  <div class="research-theme-heading">
    <p class="eyebrow">PDEs · Variational methods · Materials</p>
    <h2>Explaining macroscopic structure from microscopic defects</h2>
  </div>
  <div class="research-theme-body">
    <p>My doctoral research studied how dislocations and phase geometry influence the large-scale behaviour of crystalline materials. I developed and analysed variational models for semi-coherent interfaces, grain boundaries and two-phase composites, connecting microscopic defect mechanisms with emergent structures.</p>
    <p>This work strengthened my ability to move between physical intuition, precise mathematical formulation and asymptotic analysis—skills that remain useful far beyond materials science.</p>
    <dl class="research-contributions">
      <div><dt>Question</dt><dd>How do local defects and competing energies create observable material patterns?</dd></div>
      <div><dt>Contribution</dt><dd>Macroscopic limit models for dislocations, polycrystals and interface structure.</dd></div>
      <div><dt>Methods</dt><dd>PDEs, calculus of variations, Γ-convergence, geometric measure theory and convex integration.</dd></div>
    </dl>
    <p class="research-links-refined"><a href="publications.html#2019-Fan-Pal-Pon">SIAM Journal on Mathematical Analysis →</a><a href="publications.html">Related publications →</a></p>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="research-theme-refined" id="statistical-research">
  <div class="research-theme-number">03</div>
  <div class="research-theme-heading">
    <p class="eyebrow">Statistical learning · Sports · Decisions</p>
    <h2>Interpretable models for performance and strategy</h2>
  </div>
  <div class="research-theme-body">
    <p>At the University of Hull I developed a research strand in statistical sports modelling, closely connected to teaching and student supervision. The Formula 1 work separates driver ability from constructor strength through a time-rank duality, while the curling work combines econometric estimation, Markov modelling and simulation to quantify hammer advantage and derive strategic conditions for blanking an end.</p>
    <p>These projects show how simple, transparent models can produce useful benchmarks and decisions when data are limited and effects are confounded.</p>
    <dl class="research-contributions">
      <div><dt>Question</dt><dd>How can performance and strategic effects be separated from unequal conditions?</dd></div>
      <div><dt>Contribution</dt><dd>Interpretable probabilistic models, estimated effects, simulations and explicit decision rules.</dd></div>
      <div><dt>Methods</dt><dd>Regression, probability models, likelihood, Markov chains, simulation and model comparison.</dd></div>
    </dl>
    <p class="research-links-refined"><a href="publications.html#2024-Fry-Bri-Fan">Formula 1 paper →</a><a href="publications.html#2025-Fry-Aus-Fan">Curling paper →</a></p>
  </div>
</section>
